pull_request.title: Reclaim stale temporary indexes with age-based cleanup
pull_request.body:
Abruptly terminated commands can leave full temporary Git index copies behind. The contributor reported 52,786 files totaling 127 GB after three days of frequent statusline cancellations.

Reclaim index copies and their Git lock siblings older than one hour when a command next creates a temporary index. Keep the existing filename prefix so cleanup also handles files left by older versions. Sweep the system temp directory once per process, without making other probe threads wait, and retain best-effort cleanup in the Git-directory fallback. Normal exits still remove their own temporary indexes.

This uses age alone: no PID-tagged filenames, process checks, or platform-specific liveness behavior. Move commit-preview approval before temporary-index creation so an unattended approval prompt cannot age out an index needed afterward. The one-hour limit is a retention policy; a suspended operation or unusually slow Git filter can still exceed it. Statusline computations are unchanged.

Validation: regression tests cover stale indexes and locks, recent/future/unrelated files, both storage locations, cleanup failures, real-index preservation, and the actual approval wait. The approval test fails with the old ordering and passes with the fix. Independent review, lint, docs sync, and docs build passed. The local full gate passed 5,412 tests; three PowerShell tests failed because the installed pwsh also crashes with Stack overflow on a standalone arithmetic command outside the repository.

> _This was written by Codex on behalf of max-sixty_
pull_request.author: jonah-osmo

reviews.body: `temp_index()` is called once per worktree during `wt list` (the conflict probe in `src/commands/list/collect/tasks.rs` calls `write_tracked_worktree_tree` / `write_index_tree`, and `working_tree_diff_stats` calls it again when untracked files exist). The picker preview calls it too. Because the sweep runs inside `temp_index()`, each of those calls reads the whole system temp directory, mostly in parallel threads. That cost grows with the number of worktrees and the size of `/tmp`, and it lands on the statusline path this PR is meant to help. A per-process `Once` keeps the reclaim and cuts this to one sweep per `wt` invocation. Orphans can only come from other processes, so sweeping more often within a single process doesn't reclaim anything extra.

conversation.author: max-sixty
worktrunk-bot
conversation.body:
**Short version:** every `wt list` / `wt list statusline` run copies `.git/index` into the system temp dir once per worktree it probes. If the process is killed before it finishes, that copy stays behind. Claude Code kills slow statusline scripts as a matter of course, so on a busy machine the copies pile up. The PR deletes a copy on the next `wt` run, as soon as the PID in its name is dead. The one-day rule is only a fallback for reused PIDs.

**Where they accrue.** `WorkingTree::temp_index()` writes `$TMPDIR/worktrunk-temp-index-*` (falling back to `<gitdir>/` when the system temp dir isn't writable). Each file is a byte-for-byte copy of the worktree's index. `wt list` and the statusline call it in their conflict probes, once per worktree ([`tasks.rs`](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/commands/list/collect/tasks.rs#L609-L611)), and a second time for diff stats when untracked files exist. `wt step diff`, `step commit`/`squash`, and the picker preview also call it. The reporter's numbers fit this: 127 GB over 52,786 files is about 2.4 MB per file, against a 2.6 MB index.

**What kills `wt`.** Only `TempIndex::drop` removes the file, and destructors don't run under SIGKILL. Claude Code's [statusline docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline) say: "If a new update triggers while your script is still running, Claude Code cancels the in-flight script." The docs don't name the signal. The PR author reports it as SIGKILL; I haven't confirmed that. Either way, a statusline render that's slower than the update rate gets cancelled over and over. With ~25 sessions, each probing several worktrees, every cancellation can leave several index copies behind. OOM kills and closing the terminal leave files the same way, only less often.

**Does it delete files a `wt` process made a day ago?** Not as the main rule. A file is deleted when either:
- the PID in its name (`worktrunk-temp-index-<pid>-<random>`) no longer exists. This is the normal case, and it happens on the next `wt` run that creates a temp index, however old the file is.
- the file is older than 24 h ([`STALE_TEMP_INDEX_MAX_AGE`](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/git/repository/working_tree.rs#L26)), even if its PID is alive. This covers a PID that was reused by an unrelated process, which would otherwise keep the file forever. No `wt` command holds a temp index for more than one git probe, so a live owner never gets close to that age.

**Are they per-process?** They're narrower than that: each one lasts for a single operation, and one `wt list` creates many of them, in parallel. Today's names don't record the creating process. The PR adds the PID so the sweep can tell which files are orphans. The sweep only looks at names that match that pattern, and it runs once per process ([`AtomicBool` guard](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/git/repository/working_tree.rs#L1161)).

**Why the system temp dir rather than an XDG/worktrunk-owned path?** That choice came from #3906. Probe storage goes to system temp first so `wt list` works in read-only checkouts and writes nothing into the repo, with `.git` as the fallback. Moving the files wouldn't fix this leak, because a SIGKILL leaves the file wherever it is. A dedicated directory (e.g. under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/worktrunk/` or `<git-common-dir>/wt/`) would make cleanup simpler: the sweep could clear stale entries from a directory only worktrunk writes to, instead of scanning a shared `/tmp`, and the files would show up next to worktrunk's other state. The cost is that it needs its own read-only fallback and loses the OS's `/tmp` reaping (on systems that do it, e.g. systemd-tmpfiles' age cleanup, or a reboot). The PID-tagged sweep in this PR works the same in either location.

Two related gaps, from reading the code:
- `redirect_objects_for_observation` creates `$TMPDIR/worktrunk-list-objects-*` directories ([mod.rs](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/git/repository/mod.rs#L922)) that leak the same way under a kill, and this PR doesn't sweep them. They only hold the probe's objects, so they're probably much smaller than index copies, but they also grow without bound.
- The FAQ's "Temporary files" section still says "an interrupted process can leave one behind for manual cleanup". With this PR, that becomes true only for the object directories and for Windows, where the sweep falls back to the 24 h age check.

conversation.author: max-sixty
conversation.body:
- can we put these somewhere where the *os* will clean them up?
- even if not: can we simplify all this pid etc? no `wt` process is likely to be alive for long — maybe an alias or hook — but is there anything that could create a temp index that could be? can we just remove anything that's old, no need to look at the pid etc?
- at what cadence does this run atm? on which thread? how does the proposed code manage this?

conversation.author: worktrunk-bot
conversation.body:
**Short answers:** (1) They're already in the OS temp dir, but the OS clears it far too slowly for this leak, and git needs a real path, so there's no "delete when the process dies" option. (2) Yes, age-only works. The one thing to get right is the threshold: it trades simplicity against how many orphans pile up. (3) It sweeps once per `wt` process, synchronously, on whichever thread first creates a temp index.

**1. OS cleanup.** `temp_index()` already writes to `std::env::temp_dir()` (`$TMPDIR`, otherwise `/tmp`). OS reaping works on a scale of days. For example, this Ubuntu 24.04 runner's `/usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/tmp.conf` has `D /tmp 1777 root root 30d`, which means boot-time clearing plus a 30-day age limit. The report reached 127 GB in three days, so OS cleanup alone doesn't contain it. The kind of file the kernel removes when its owner dies (an unlinked or `O_TMPFILE` file, or delete-on-close on Windows) doesn't work here either. Git needs `GIT_INDEX_FILE` to be a named path, because it writes the index by creating a `<path>.lock` sibling and renaming it over the original.

**2. Age-only.** No current holder lives long:
- `wt list` and statusline probes, plus the picker preview, hold one for milliseconds to seconds.
- `wt step commit --dry-run` and `wt step squash --dry-run` hold one across the LLM call ([commit.rs](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/commands/step/commit.rs#L102), [squash.rs](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/commands/step/squash.rs#L555)). That's seconds to minutes.
- `wt step diff` keeps the file alive for as long as the user sits in git's pager ([diff.rs](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/commands/step/diff.rs#L44)). Git loads the index before it starts paging, though, so deleting it at that point should be harmless.

Hooks and aliases run as child processes and never receive a temp index, so a long-running hook doesn't matter here.

The real hazard with age-only is deleting the file while a git command is about to read it. That fails silently instead of with an error: git treats a missing `GIT_INDEX_FILE` as an empty index. I checked this. `GIT_INDEX_FILE=<missing> git write-tree` returns the empty tree `4b825dc…`, and `git diff --cached` shows every file as deleted. So the threshold needs to sit well above the longest hold, and even a short one like 10–60 minutes clears that.

What the PID check buys is a shorter steady state. Under age-only, orphans build up to roughly threshold × leak rate. The report's rate (127 GB over three days) works out to about 1.8 GB per hour, so a 1-hour threshold would leave about 1.8 GB on that machine and the PR's current 24 h about 42 GB. The PID check reclaims an orphan on the next run instead. Without it, the change drops `temp_index_prefix_for`, `temp_index_owner_pid`, both `process_is_alive` variants, and the PID in the file name. The sweep becomes "prefix matches and mtime is older than N". I'd take that simplification with a short threshold (~1 h), unless the remaining GB on heavy machines matters to you.

**3. Cadence.** The sweep runs inside `temp_index()`, guarded by a process-wide `AtomicBool` ([working_tree.rs#L1161-L1164](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/git/repository/working_tree.rs#L1161-L1164)):
- **Which commands:** only those that create a temp index: `wt list` / statusline when they run the conflict or diff probes, `wt step diff`, `step commit` / `squash --dry-run`, and the picker preview. Other commands never sweep.
- **Which thread:** in `wt list`, the first parallel worker to reach `temp_index()` sweeps synchronously before creating its own file. The other workers see the flag already set and continue without waiting. That one probe takes the hit.
- **Cost:** one `read_dir` of the temp dir, comparing names by prefix, then a `stat`, a `kill(pid, 0)`, and possibly an `unlink` for each worktrunk-named file. Once orphans are cleared, that's a single directory listing per process. The exception is the first run on a machine like the reporter's: it has to unlink tens of thousands of files inside a statusline render, which may itself get killed. It still makes progress each time, because every unlink sticks.
- **Fallback path:** when the system temp dir isn't writable, the `<gitdir>` fallback sweeps `<gitdir>` on every such call ([L1168](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/git/repository/working_tree.rs#L1168)). That path isn't behind the `AtomicBool`. The directory is small, so it's cheap, but it isn't once per process.

conversation.author: max-sixty
conversation.body:
one more idea: why are we producing so many & large temp index files? I thought these were really small? is there anything we can do there?

would much rather rely on OS cleanups than managing it ourselves, if possible

conversation.author: worktrunk-bot
conversation.body:
**Short version:** each copy is the whole index, and an index holds about 100 bytes for every tracked file. It's small in a small repo; the reporter's 2.6 MB index means roughly 25k tracked files. We can cut how often copies are made, and on the statusline path we can stop making them, which is the lever that would let OS cleanup be enough. Making each copy smaller isn't practical.

**Why each copy is large.** Git has no partial index. `write-tree` and `diff` read the full one, so a copy has to be the full one too. I measured a 2,000-file repo at 207 KB, about 103 B per entry (stat data, OID, and path). We copy rather than use the real index because `git write-tree` on the real index takes `index.lock`. With a lock present it fails with `fatal: Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists` (checked on git 2.55). That would fight with the user's own git and with agents running git in the same worktree.

**Why there are so many.** The statusline renders one worktree but runs every `wt list` task ([`statusline_options`](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/commands/statusline.rs#L867)). A worktree with changes gets up to two copies per render:
- the working-tree conflict probe, when tracked files changed ([tasks.rs#L609](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/commands/list/collect/tasks.rs#L609)): copy, `add -u`, `write-tree`, then `merge-tree`
- the diff stats, when untracked files exist ([tasks.rs#L491](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/60feb4f72d89a02f635d65d9afdac648aeccfb61/src/commands/list/collect/tasks.rs#L491)): untracked paths are added to the copy as intent-to-add, so renames pair up

A worktree an agent is editing nearly always meets both conditions. A copy leaks only if the render is killed partway. Claude Code [debounces updates at 300 ms and cancels an in-flight script when a new update fires](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline#how-status-lines-work). So while an agent is streaming, any render slower than the update rate gets cancelled again and again, and each cancellation can leave ~5 MB behind. Across ~25 sessions that adds up to the reported 52k files.

**What we could do, roughly in order of effect:**
1. **Drop the working-tree conflict probe from the statusline.** It does the most git work in the render (it re-hashes modified files, writes a tree, and runs a merge), so dropping it should make renders faster and less likely to be cancelled. It also removes one copy per render. The statusline would fall back to the commit-based conflict check that clean worktrees already use. The cost is that uncommitted edits that would conflict no longer show in the statusline; `wt list` still shows them.
2. **Count untracked lines without a temp index on the statusline**, giving up rename pairing there. This removes the other copy. It changes the numbers for a moved file that hasn't been staged (shown as +N/−N rather than as a rename).
3. **Share one copy between the two tasks**, which halves the copies. It couples two parallel tasks, so it's the least appealing.

With 1 and 2, the statusline creates no temp index at all, so there's nothing on that path for a cancellation to leave behind. The remaining leaks would come from a killed `wt list`, `wt step diff`, or the picker, which are interactive and rarely SIGKILLed. At that rate, the OS's `/tmp` cleanup (reboot, or tmpfiles age-out) would be enough, and this PR's sweep could be dropped or cut down to the age-only version.

I haven't measured where the reporter's render time goes. A `wt -vv list statusline` profile from their machine would confirm whether the conflict probe is what pushes renders past the cancellation window. If 1 and 2 sound right, I can open a PR for them.

<details><summary>Dead ends checked</summary>

- **Hardlinking instead of copying.** Git writes an index through `<path>.lock` plus a rename, so a hardlinked copy would be safe. But the link has to be on the same filesystem as `.git`, which puts the files back in the repo, where the OS never cleans them up.
- **Delete-on-exit files (`O_TMPFILE`, `/proc/self/fd/N`).** Git needs a path where it can create a `.lock` sibling. `write-tree` and `add -u` both write the index back that way.
- **Split index.** The shared half lives in `.git` and has its own expiry. It's a lot of machinery for a probe.

</details>
